Avondale's tap water is a blend of Colorado River water and local groundwater, and both end up in your pool. Call the free line any hour to be put through to an independent, locally owned pool company that works in Avondale.

Pool service in Avondale, AZ starts with what comes out of the hose. This West Valley city mixes Colorado River water with water pumped from its own wells, and that blend is what you top your pool off with all summer. Below: what that blend means for an Avondale pool, plus the way a single free phone call links you with pool help nearby.

Avondale: two water sources in one pool

The City of Avondale runs its own water utility. Part of the supply is groundwater, pumped from a network of city wells that reach the West Salt River Valley Sub-Basin aquifer. The other part is surface water from the Colorado River, which Avondale receives under an agreement with the City of Phoenix. Phoenix delivers Avondale's allocation through its regional pipeline system, and the city blends it with well water before it reaches homes.

For a pool owner, the practical point is that you are not working with one fixed kind of water. Groundwater and river water carry different amounts of dissolved minerals, so the water you add in July may not match what you added in March. A pool that held steady for years can start leaving white crust at the waterline after a long run of hot days and heavy top offs. That is a good reason to have the pool water itself tested on a regular schedule rather than relying on a number from a report.

Pool service Avondale AZ homeowners ask about

Most calls are for steady pool service: someone to skim, brush, empty baskets and keep the chemistry in range through the hottest months. Mineral crust on the waterline tile is common wherever hard water evaporates, and tile cleaning covers how it is removed without damaging the tile. A filter that loads up quickly after dusty weather calls for pool filter cleaning. And if the pool drops faster than the heat explains, or the water bill climbs with it, pool leak repair explains how a leak is found.

Reading Avondale's water report for your pool

The city publishes its water test results once a year in a Consumer Confidence Report. The report covering January through December 2025 was posted in June 2026.

Where to find it

The Water Quality page on the city's website links each year's report, with older reports kept in an archive. Paper copies are available at Avondale City Hall and local libraries.

What to look for

Look for the rows that describe minerals, such as hardness, sodium or total dissolved solids (TDS), the overall amount of minerals and salts dissolved in the water. For a pool, these are the figures that shape how fast scale forms.

What it cannot tell you

The report describes water leaving the system, not water that has sat in your pool for two summers. Evaporation leaves minerals behind, so the pool's own test numbers matter more than the tap figures.

When the water bill and the pool both look wrong

If your pool has an automatic filler, it is a valve with a float that adds water whenever the level drops. It saves you from dragging a hose out every few days. It can also hide a problem. The city's utility billing FAQ points out that pool fillers, water softeners, water filters and water heaters all have floats that can stick open and run water you never see. Its suggestion is simple: turn the device off and repeat the meter test. If the usage stops, you have found the source.

That matters more now that water costs more. Avondale adopted new water, sewer and solid waste rates that took effect January 1, 2026, and the city adds a 7.5 percent water treatment fee and a 6.2 percent water resource fee to the total water bill. A filler stuck open, or a slow leak in the plumbing, is paying those fees on water that ends up in the ground.

Safe checks before you call

  • Water level. Note where the water sits on the skimmer opening, then check again in a day with the filler turned off.
  • Equipment pad. Look for drips, damp soil or white mineral trails on the pump, filter and pipes.
  • Baskets and gauge. Empty the skimmer and pump baskets and write down the filter pressure reading.
  • Breaker. If the pump is dead, reset a tripped breaker or GFCI once. If it trips again, leave it off and call.
  • Home test kit. Test the water and keep the numbers to read out on the call.

Safety first. Never mix pool chemicals with each other, and store them apart, dry, shaded and out of children's reach. Keep children away from any pool that is not fenced or covered. A cloudy or green pool is a drowning hazard because no one can see the bottom. If you smell gas near a pool heater, leave the area, do not touch switches or the heater, and from a safe distance call 911 or the emergency number on your gas bill.

Draining, power and questions to ask

Sooner or later, high mineral levels push many Valley pool owners toward a partial or full drain. Before any water leaves your yard, find out where it is allowed to go. This page could not confirm Avondale's current rules on pool draining and filter backwash, so ask the city first. AviWise, the city's online service portal, is where residents report issues and request city services, and it is a sensible place to ask. The guide on how often to drain a pool in Arizona covers the questions to settle first.

For power, most Valley homes are served by APS or SRP depending on the address, so check the name on your bill if a pump or heater has no power and the house does. Neither utility repairs pool equipment.

Questions to ask an Avondale pool company

  • What is your Arizona ROC license number? Ask for repair, equipment and resurfacing work, then check it yourself.
  • Can you test for calcium hardness and TDS on every visit? Those two numbers show whether the blend is building scale.
  • Will you check the auto filler? A float that sticks can waste water before anyone notices.
  • If the pool needs draining, where will the water go? Ask how the company follows the city's rules.
  • What does the quote include? Get labor, parts and chemicals listed before work begins.

Common questions

Where does Avondale get its water?

From two places. The City of Avondale pumps groundwater from wells that draw on the West Salt River Valley Sub-Basin aquifer, and it receives Colorado River water through an agreement with the City of Phoenix, which moves Avondale's share through its regional pipelines. What reaches your hose is a blend of the two.

Is Avondale water hard enough to cause scale in a pool?

The city publishes its test results every year in its Water Quality Report, which is the place to look for the mineral figures at your tap. In a pool, though, the tap number is only the start: water evaporates, the minerals stay behind, and every top off adds more. Testing the pool itself for calcium hardness is what tells you whether scale is building.

Why did my Avondale water bill jump in the summer?

An automatic pool filler is one possible cause. The city's utility billing FAQ notes that pool fillers, like water softeners and water heaters, have floats that can stick open. Its advice is to turn the device off and repeat the meter test. If the meter stops moving, you have found the source. A leak in the pool itself is another possibility, and that is work for a pool company.

Can I drain my pool into the street in Avondale?

Do not assume so. This page could not confirm Avondale's current rules on where pool and backwash water may go, so ask the city before you drain, through its AviWise service portal, and ask the pool company how it plans to handle the water.

Do I need a licensed contractor for pool work in Avondale?

For repairs, equipment replacement and resurfacing, Arizona generally expects a contractor licensed by the Registrar of Contractors, whose residential classifications include R-6, Swimming Pool Service and Repair. Whether a cleaning-only service needs a license is not spelled out, so ask the ROC if that matters to you. Ask the company for its ROC license number and look it up on the ROC contractor search before work starts.
